name: Gamāle Khām
confidence_why: Wilde 2011 says outright that Gamāle Khām stress is "yet to be determined with any certainty", Wilde 2016 and Wilde 2017 describe phonation and report the language as atonal without ever locating word stress, and Watters 1973 treats Takāle Khām clause syntax and never mentions Gamāle, so no published description says where, or whether, this language stresses words.

catalog_quote: [Wilde 2016 §2.3, p.135] Gamāle Khām contrasts between modal (14a) and breathy (14b) phonation. ... In Wilde (2011: 279,287) I considered whether Gamāle Khām phonology may also feature tense phonation. However, further investigation has led to the conclusion that this is not the case, and that the stiff voice or laryngealisation is an idiolectal tendency and/or caused variably by syllable-final glottal restriction. Unlike Takāle Khām as described by Watters (1971; 1985; 2002), Gamāle Khām is an atonal language. A pitch distinction was encountered with any certainty only once in the corpus (15a–b). ... tone_statements.citation: Wilde, Christopher P. (2011). Observations on the phonology of Gamāle Khām. Himalayan Linguistics Journal 10. pp. 273-290.
tone_statements.quote: Tense phonation always has a pitch which is relatively higher than for words with modal or breathy phonation. In addition, certain of the words identified thus far, such as (47a-b), (48a-b) and (49a-b), do seem to have a pitch distinction. [...] Whether high pitch in (47b), (48b) and (49b) is caused by tense phonation, or vice versa, is yet to be determined. In the latter case it would be tone, and not tense phonation, which would be considered to be phonemic. [...] the reason for positing three phonation types in Gamāle – rather than two phonation types and one tone distinction – is because no contour contrasts have thus far been indentified.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 4 'Notes on phonation types and tone', pp. 287-288 as printed (Himalayan Linguistics 10(1))

audit.reasoning: The record codes Gamale Kham not determinable because none of the three dedicated phonological descriptions (Wilde 2011, 2016, 2017) states, locates or denies word stress; I re-opened all three held texts at the cited loci and confirmed every quoted sentence verbatim with correct page numbers, and a full-text search for stress/accent confirm 'stress' appears only in the 2011 abstract disclaimer and a Takale clitic gloss in 2017. These are the best and only phonological sources for this languoid per Glottolog and a Crossref search; the remaining unheld items (Moore 2019 MA morphology thesis; Wilde 2017 LTBA historical paper) are unlikely to contain a stress rule. Nothing was downloaded beyond bibliographic records (saved with; Coding and strength of the evidence stand; no action.

sources.note: Describes Kham of the Taka-Sera (Takale) area, Baglung District — i.e. Takāle / Western Parbate Kham, not Gamāle Khām of Rolpā. It is also silent on stress, so it neither agrees with nor contradicts the (empty) catalog record.

sources.citation: Wilde, Christopher P. (2011). Observations on the phonology of Gamāle Khām. Himalayan Linguistics Journal 10. pp. 273-290.
sources.note: The catalog record for Gamāle Khām has an empty rule; Wilde 2011 gives no placement either, only the statement that stress patterns are yet to be determined and that a phonation/pitch (possibly tonal) contrast exists on words. The only 'stress' passage beyond the abstract is fn. 13 (p. 288) quoting Watters 2002: 38 on Takāle Khām tones T-1/T-2 being associated with 'intensity or stress' vs 'a lack of laryngeal stress' — that is about Takāle, not Gamāle, and about laryngeal register, not word-stress placement.

tone.says: Sec. 4 'Notes on phonation types and tone' (pp. 286-288): Gamale has three phonation types (modal, breathy, tense) with pitch correlates (breathy = lower, tense = higher pitch); a few minimal pairs differ only in mid vs high pitch; whether pitch or tense phonation is the phonemic property 'is yet to be determined'; no contour contrasts found, unlike Watters' Takale four-box register x melody system (reproduced as Fig. 3); tone left for further research.
